# Sign Language Recognition and Generation: Datasets, Architectures, and Emerging Directions

Sign language processing research spans two primary tasks: recognition (sign-to-text) and generation (text-to-sign), with recognition receiving substantially more attention to date (Bao2026 pages 2-3). For continuous sign language recognition (CSLR), traditional architectures follow a three-stage pipeline: spatial feature extraction via 2D-CNNs, 3D-CNNs, GCNs, or transformers; temporal modeling using 1D-CNNs, spatio-temporal GCNs, RNNs, or transformers; and sequence alignment through CTC, correlation maps, reinforcement learning, or HMMs (Johnny2025 pages 2-3). These alignment-based methods have notable limitations—CTC approaches often overfit and suffer error propagation, while HMM-based methods require small vocabularies (Johnny2025 pages 2-3).

Recent work addresses these constraints through alternative architectures. AutoSign introduces an autoregressive decoder-only transformer paired with 1D CNN temporal compression to directly translate pose sequences to text, bypassing gloss annotations and alignment mechanisms entirely; it leverages AraGPT2 for Arabic text generation and demonstrates improved WER on the Isharah-1000 Saudi Sign Language dataset (Johnny2025 pages 1-2, Johnny2025 pages 2-3).

Dataset development remains critical to progress. Resources include PHOENIX-2014T and How2Sign for recognition (Bao2026 pages 2-3), alongside Brazilian Sign Language corpora (VLibrasBD, MINDS-Libras, LIBRAS-UFOP, LSWH100, ICSL) and specialized collections like PopSign and LIBRAS-UFSC (Boddu2026 pages 3-4). Landmark detection tools such as MediaPipe and OpenPose support real-time recognition in constrained environments (Boddu2026 pages 3-4).

Generation systems have remained predominantly monolingual, typically processing only English input (Bao2026 pages 2-3). CSF addresses this gap by enabling direct multilingual-to-sign-language translation without English as an intermediary, using a nine-slot semantic schema and achieving 99.03% extraction accuracy with a compact, efficient model (Bao2026 pages 8-9).

evidence.context: AutoSign proposes an autoregressive decoder-only transformer combined with a 1D CNN temporal compression module for continuous sign language recognition (CSLR), directly translating pose sequences to Arabic text without intermediate gloss supervision. It bypasses traditional CTC/HMM alignment-based pipelines, uses AraGPT2 (pre-trained Arabic decoder transformer) for text generation, and applies CNNs to compress pose sequences before decoding. The model achieves improved Word Error Rate (WER) on the Isharah-1000 dataset (Saudi Sign Language), showing hand and body gestures are most discriminative for signer-independent CSLR.
evidence.citation: Johnny, Samuel Ebimobowei, et al. "AutoSign: Direct Pose-to-Text Translation for Continuous Sign Language Recognition." *arXiv*, 26 July 2025, arXiv:2507.19840.

evidence.context: Traditional CSLR architectures have three stages: spatial feature extraction using 2D-CNNs, 3D-CNNs, GCNs, or transformers; temporal modeling using 1D-CNNs, spatio-temporal GCNs, RNNs, or transformers; and sequence alignment using CTC, correlation maps, reinforcement learning, or HMMs. CTC-based approaches often overfit and suffer error propagation, while HMM-based methods need small vocabularies. AutoSign proposes a decoder-only transformer for end-to-end autoregressive pose-to-text translation, using 1D CNNs for temporal compression, avoiding gloss annotations and alignment mechanisms, tested on the Isharah Arabic Sign Language dataset.

evidence.context: This paper introduces a training pipeline for Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) using image/video augmentations and an IoU-balanced classification loss with an added regression head to handle low data quality and varying sign speeds. It achieves state-of-the-art results on WLASL and Slovo datasets. The introduction discusses challenges in SLR: variability in gesturing speed, complex spatial-temporal features, limited high-quality datasets, and real-world conditions like lighting/background. It distinguishes ISLR, CSLR, and SLT tasks within sign language understanding.
evidence.citation: Kvanchiani, Karina, et al. "Training Strategies for Isolated Sign Language Recognition." *arXiv*, 12 May 2025, arXiv:2412.11553.

evidence.context: The excerpt describes CSF (Contrastive Semantic Features), a framework for direct multilingual-to-sign-language translation that bypasses English as an intermediary. It uses a nine-slot semantic schema for sign language grammar, a 35-class condition taxonomy, and achieves 99.03% extraction accuracy with a compact 0.74 MB model and 3.02ms real-time inference. References include foundational neural sign language translation work , How2Sign dataset, cross-lingual representation learning (XLM-R), language-agnostic BERT embeddings, Transformer architecture (Attention is All You Need), and BPE subword tokenization—key components underlying neural network-based sign language translation systems.
evidence.citation: Bao, Tran Sy. "CSF: Contrastive Semantic Features for Direct Multilingual Sign Language Generation." 2026.
